title: Linear-time directed bottleneck paths and trees
formal: Do the directed bottleneck path and rooted bottleneck spanning-tree problems admit comparison-based algorithms with expected running time \(O(n+m)\) on every input, always returning an exact optimum? The input has \(n\) vertices and \(m\) weighted directed edges. Randomization is allowed; deterministic linear time would also answer positively. The source writes \(O(m)\) after the usual removal or treatment of irrelevant vertices. The requested guarantee is total running time, including graph processing and output, with weights accessible only through comparisons.
context:
Theorem 3 gives expected O(mβ(m,n)) time, where β(m,n) is the least k≥1 for which the k-times iterated base-two logarithm of n is at most m/n, in the nondegenerate regime m≥n. This overhead grows very slowly, and the theorem is already linear when m≥n log^(k)n for any fixed k. The question includes sparse graphs where β is unbounded.

The source already obtains deterministic linear time in the word-RAM model and recalls linear-time algorithms for undirected graphs. Its open question concerns arbitrary directed graphs with opaque comparison-only weights.

Section 4 relates the two problems at the expected-linear scale. The spanning-tree objective is one global bottleneck; it should not be replaced with the stronger requirement to return every single-source optimal bottleneck path.

Gorbachev’s August 2026 preprint gives a counterexample to the 2016 paper’s claimed linear-time algorithm for deterministic graphical games and a linear reduction from directed BP to the designated-start game-value problem. It explicitly retains the BP question. This correction concerns the DGG claim, not the paper’s stated randomized BP/BST upper bound or its word-RAM result.
why: Determines the exact cost of fundamental directed min-max optimization when numerical information is available only by comparison. Removing the overhead would close a long-standing gap for sparse graphs; distinguishing the input model prevents an already-solved variant from being presented as open.
status_note: Checked the original definitions, Theorem 3, both reductions, the word-RAM result and the exact Section 7 questions, plus the August 2026 v2 preprint including its counterexample and reduction statement. The main target permits always-correct randomization, matching the preceding expected-time theorem; the separate deterministic near-linear question is not silently substituted. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The recent correction is a preprint and its proofs were not independently audited.

references.title: Bottleneck Paths and Trees and Deterministic Graphical Games
references.authors: Chechik, Shiri; Kaplan, Haim; Thorup, Mikkel; Zamir, Or; Zwick, Uri
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 12; PDF page 12

definitions:
In the bottleneck path problem (BP), the input is an explicit directed graph G=(V,E), a source s, a target t and a weight w(e) for every edge. Among all directed s-to-t paths P, output one minimizing max_{e∈P}w(e). Any optimal simple path is acceptable; ties require no prescribed choice. If t is unreachable, report that no path exists. When s=t the empty path is returned, with bottleneck conventionally −∞.

In the bottleneck spanning-tree problem (BST), the input is the same kind of directed weighted graph and a specified root s. Output an out-arborescence T spanning all vertices: s has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one in T, and there is a directed path in T from s to every vertex. Minimize max_{e∈T}w(e). If no such tree exists, report this. For a one-vertex graph, the empty tree has value −∞. This objective minimizes the single largest tree-edge weight, not the sum of weights. A tree minimizing that largest weight need not supply an individually optimal bottleneck path to every vertex.

Weights are arbitrary elements of a totally ordered set, such as arbitrary real numbers. They are opaque keys: they may be stored, copied and compared in constant time, but their digits, arithmetic values and integer ranks are not available for computation. Equal weights are allowed. The graph is given by adjacency lists with O(log(n+m+2))-bit vertex and edge indices; ordinary operations on these indices have unit cost. The algorithm is charged for all graph operations, comparisons, random sampling and writing its path or tree, not just the number of comparisons. There is no assumption that the weights are sorted, bounded integers, or machine words supporting bit operations.

The randomization convention is Las Vegas: on every fixed input the answer is exact, termination occurs with probability one, and the expected total work over the algorithm's internal random choices is at most C(n+m) for a universal constant C. This includes feasibility checks and output. A randomized algorithm with a small probability of an incorrect optimum would not meet this convention. For BP, isolated and unreachable vertices can be removed in O(n+m) work. A feasible nontrivial BST instance has m≥n−1. Thus O(n+m) makes the source's O(m) target meaningful also on degenerate explicit inputs without changing its substantive content.

The question asks for this guarantee for both tasks, but their expected-linear-time versions are equivalent through the reductions in Section 4 of the source. These reductions do not establish the corresponding deterministic equivalence: the BST-to-BP reduction uses randomness. The source's separate question about a deterministic O(mβ(m,n)) bound is not the target of this card. Neither all-pairs bottleneck paths nor finding every individual single-source bottleneck value is required.
answer_criterion: Give always-correct comparison-based algorithms with expected O(n+m) total work for both directed tasks, or use the source reductions to derive both guarantees from one. Alternatively, rule out such algorithms, stating any assumptions used. An undirected algorithm, a word-RAM algorithm inspecting weight representations, a bound on comparisons alone, or a faster algorithm only for sufficiently dense graphs does not settle the unrestricted target. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the permitted randomized algorithms.
